title: Small hospital, bigger swings?
hook: A small hospital and a big one, same chance of a boy. Do they see the same extremes?

knows: that about half of babies are boys
doesNotKnow: how sample size changes the spread of a percentage

misconception: A small group and a large group are equally likely to show an extreme percentage, because the underlying chance is the same.
objective: The learner can explain that percentages from small samples swing more widely, so extreme results (like more than 60% boys) turn up more often in small groups.

claims.text: With 15 births a day and each baby a boy with probability 1/2, the chance that more than 60% are boys (10 or more) is 4,944/32,768, about 15.1%, or about 55 days a year.
With 45 births a day, the chance that more than 60% are boys (28 or more) is about 6.8%, or about 25 days a year.
claims.source: P(X >= 28), X ~ Binomial(45, 1/2) = 0.0676 (exact sum in node; model.ts exactOver60(45)); x 365 = 24.7.

claims.text: In the stage's seeded year, hospital A (15 a day) had 53 days over 60% boys and hospital B (45 a day) had 30.
claims.source: src/demos/probability/small-hospital-big-swings/model.ts year(n), seed 1974 x 1000 + n. Re-run: 15 -> 53 days, 45 -> 30, 5 -> 73, 25 -> 46, 100 -> 3.

claims.text: The hospital question (15 vs 45 births a day, days with more than 60% boys) comes from Tversky and Kahneman, and most people they asked answered 'about the same'.
claims.source: A. Tversky and D. Kahneman (1974), 'Judgment under uncertainty: Heuristics and biases', Science 185(4157): 1124-1131, section on insensitivity to sample size (originally D. Kahneman and A. Tversky (1972), 'Subjective probability: A judgment of representativeness', Cognitive Psychology 3: 430-454).

claims.text: Real births are about 51% boys; the lesson uses 50% as a simplification.
claims.source: The human sex ratio at birth is about 105 boys per 100 girls (51.2% boys): United Nations, World Population Prospects (sex ratio at birth); the 50% figure is the convention of the original problem.

recall.question: The schools with the very highest average test scores in a country are mostly tiny schools. What is the likeliest explanation?
options: Small groups' averages swing more, so they fill both extremes
Big schools hide their best pupils
recall.why: Averages of a few pupils vary much more than averages of many. Tiny schools show up at the top and at the bottom of the rankings.
